AI-Native
Organization
Handbook
Choose useful work, give people clear ownership, and test
whether agent workflows improve delivery.
Michael Long
October 23, 2026 · Version 1.1.0
Expanded edition

ii
Make a better
delivery decision
Your team can generate a change quickly and still struggle to deliver it.
Someone has to decide whether the change matters, resolve conflicting
requirements, review the result, release it and support the customer
afterward. Giving agents more execution work leaves those
responsibilities with people.
This handbook helps engineering and product leaders decide where
agent workflows can improve delivery. Here, AI-native describes an
organization that keeps the information, tools and safeguards people
and agents need in working order. The test is whether customers receive
better outcomes at an acceptable total cost.
Begin with one existing team and one recurring customer need. Chapter
1 helps you select the work and assign ownership. Chapter 2 turns
delegation into a workflow the team can operate. Chapter 3 shows how to
fund a comparison, read the results and choose a limited next
investment. Two worksheets help you apply the decisions.
Chapter 3 walks through a team's decision about whether a new
workflow is worth funding. The numbers are illustrative; the questions
are the ones you'll need to answer before committing money or changing
how your team works.

1
CHAPTER 01
Choose useful work and
clear owners
Start with a customer problem and the dependency that holds it
back. Keep responsibility clear as execution changes.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
1. CHOOSE USEFUL WORK AND CLEAR OWNERS
2
Find the constraint worth changing
Choose recurring customer work that the team already needs to deliver
and understands well enough to judge. Divide it into independently
testable changes so the team can obtain feedback before committing to a
larger intervention. [S9]
For saved searches, customers need to save a query, find it later and
keep it private across web and mobile. If changes spend days waiting for
an interface decision, faster code generation leaves the main delay
intact. Match the intervention to where recent changes actually waited.
 Where does the change wait?
 Repeated interface
 clarification
 Agree an interface
 contract
 Routine mobile
implementation or
 review
 Evaluate a reusable
 workflow
 Unresolved product
 choice
 Name an owner and
 resolve it
Look at a few recent changes from the initial request through production
use. Where did people spend time working, waiting or redoing work?
Who resolved difficult decisions? Include review, customer observation
and recovery so the intervention addresses the delay the team actually
experiences.
Make the expected benefit specific enough to test: "For routine
saved-search changes, clearer interface agreements and reusable
automation that has been tested will reduce recurring delivery cost
while preserving customer success and quality." The proposal names the
work, the improvement and the conditions the team cannot sacrifice to
get it.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
1. CHOOSE USEFUL WORK AND CLEAR OWNERS
3
Give one team the whole outcome
Give one product team responsibility for the customer journey from
problem selection through maintenance. For saved searches, the team
owns the experience across clients, persistence, privacy, release and
incident response. Delegating work leaves that responsibility with the
team.
 The product team owns the whole outcome
 PRODUCT TEAM
 Define the work
 Customer problem, scope
 and privacy
 DELEGATED WORKFLOW
 Execute within limits
 Implementation within
contracts; tests, checks
and maintained context
 PRODUCT TEAM
 Accept and support
 Acceptance, release,
production support and
 recovery
 Review the evidence; decide what happens next.
The team still needs access to named specialists for unfamiliar
architecture, unresolved accessibility failures and work outside its
authority. Sharing specialists can reduce duplication, but teams may
have to wait for them. Embedding specialists makes help easier to
obtain, at a staffing and coordination cost. Before changing team
composition, find out whether people can get the help they need during
ordinary work, urgent reviews and incidents.
For the first trial, keep staffing, reporting lines and release responsibility
stable. Change how the team obtains context and executes a defined
class of work, then use the result to inform the next decision.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
1. CHOOSE USEFUL WORK AND CLEAR OWNERS
4
Make the responsibility clear enough that people know whom to call:
"The Search team owns customers' ability to save and reuse searches,
including production support; the mobile specialist owns decisions
about unfamiliar native interaction patterns." Use real team and owner
names before launch.
Assign the decisions people retain
Name people for these responsibilities before granting a workflow
access. One person may hold several roles in a small team. Keep release
authority and the ability to challenge a result explicit.
Reserve time for reviewing unfamiliar work, handling escalations and
recovering from incidents. Name a backup for each decision owner, with
access to the same context and records. If neither owner is available,
pause work that needs their approval until an authorized person can
review it.
When a shared workflow introduces a defect, its maintainer corrects the
workflow. The product team restores the affected feature, for example
by rolling back a faulty saved-search release and checking that
customers can save and reopen queries. The platform owner handles
any infrastructure or access failure.
DECISION OWNER
WHAT THE OWNER DECIDES AND MAINTAINS
Product team
Which customer problem to solve; acceptance, release, production
support and maintenance of its product area.
Product / design lead
What customer success means; representative observations and
whether the delivered experience is useful.
Workflow maintainer
Instructions, context assembly, model/tool versions, workflow
evaluations and controlled capability changes.
Specialist
Domain rules, unfamiliar technical tradeoffs and exceptions
requiring expertise beyond routine checks.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
1. CHOOSE USEFUL WORK AND CLEAR OWNERS
5
DECISION OWNER
WHAT THE OWNER DECIDES AND MAINTAINS
Platform / security owner
Task identities, access enforcement, environments, audit records,
revocation and infrastructure recovery.
Measurement owner
Task allocation, complete cost and outcome records, missing
evidence and preserved analysis snapshots.
Sponsor
Funding, permitted risk within their authority, and the recorded
decision to continue, stop or fund replication.
Make shared expertise usable
A shared agent workflow needs the same care as a service that teams
depend on. Explain which tasks it supports, what information it needs,
what it checks and when users should ask for help. Teams need both a
reliable way to do routine work and a way to reach a specialist when the
workflow cannot handle it.
A mobile capability might supply current interface patterns, an
implementation workflow and accessibility checks. Its maintainer owns
those reusable elements. The product team supplies the customer goal
and judges the resulting experience. A novel navigation pattern goes to a
specialist before routine automation proceeds.
Start with work that several teams repeatedly need. Count the cost of
building and maintaining the shared capability, along with support
hours, time waiting for review and accepted outcomes. Reuse pays off
when it helps teams finish useful work with less total effort and expense.
The number of times a workflow runs cannot tell you that on its own.
If routine changes still wait for the enabling team, inspect the reason. A
missing test needs a test; an obsolete rule needs a context correction; a
mandatory specialist decision needs capacity or a narrower scope. Each
correction is more concrete than adding another review agent.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
1. CHOOSE USEFUL WORK AND CLEAR OWNERS
6
When many teams depend on one workflow, one defect can affect them
all. Keep its version fixed during a comparison. Test a replacement with
a limited group of users, identify the work it affects and keep a rollback
available. Teams should know how to continue delivery if the shared
workflow is unavailable.
Fund broader reuse after teams can operate the capability and its
support burden is understood. A workflow that succeeds only when its
author sits beside the user is still being developed.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
1. CHOOSE USEFUL WORK AND CLEAR OWNERS
7
Match the structure to your
coordination needs
Start with the dependencies between customer outcomes, the specialists
people need, and the decisions each team can make alone. Add shared
coordination where it helps teams finish work.
These four arrangements are proposals. The sizes are illustrative
total-company headcounts, including non-engineering roles. They are
not engineering headcounts, staffing ratios or thresholds for
reorganizing.
People retain responsibility for outcomes and release; this does not
require manual approval of every routine deployment.
Boxes group work, not reporting lines. Solid arrows show work, priorities or evidence; dashed arrows
show support or controls.
A small company may coordinate one multidisciplinary team through
direct conversation and one backlog. The same people can maintain its
tools and workflows.
Around 10 people: one team
FOUNDERS + CORE TEAM

1. CHOOSE USEFUL WORK AND CLEAR OWNERS
8
When several product teams need the same help, give them shared
workflow support and access to specialists. Keep those services usable
without making every delivery wait in one central queue.

Product leadership

9
When dependencies cluster around a product domain, a domain lead can
coordinate priorities and interfaces across teams. Each team still owns
its customer outcome and release; the platform and specialist
communities support that work.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
1. CHOOSE USEFUL WORK AND CLEAR OWNERS
10
Business units with different markets or operating needs may need more
local authority. Local capability hubs maintain context, evaluations and
domain tools, while an enterprise foundation supplies common controls.
Name the cross-unit agreements and escalation routes. Domain
coordination within each unit is omitted here for clarity.
Around 10,000 people: federated units
Enterprise foundation
Identity / security / audit / standards
BUSINESS UNIT A
PRODUCT TEAMS
Owner /
release
Agents
Local capability hub
BUSINESS UNIT B
PRODUCT TEAMS
Owner /
release
Agents
Local capability hub
Contracts / escalation
Before changing reporting lines, trace a few delayed changes across
team boundaries. Decide whether the problem needs a clearer interface,
more available specialist time, a shared service or a different decision
owner. Test that change before applying a larger reorganization.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
1. CHOOSE USEFUL WORK AND CLEAR OWNERS
11
Protect judgment and attention
A team needs enough expertise to challenge the work it accepts. Before
delegating a task, name who can explain the affected architecture,
recognize a consequential error and restore service. Availability on an
organization chart is insufficient if the specialist has no capacity during
review or an incident.
Reserve human time for product decisions, review, exceptions and
learning. More parallel agent runs create more proposed work to
inspect. Limit work in progress when the review queue grows, and
measure the waiting time and rework that follow each additional run.
Use review to expose assumptions. For saved searches, a reviewer
should be able to explain why one customer cannot read another's saved
query, how a failed save appears and what happens after an interface
version changes. Agreement between agents cannot supply that
explanation by itself.
Maintain opportunities for engineers to investigate failures and work
through complete changes. Specialists should improve reusable rules
and help others develop judgment, while remaining available for
difficult cases. Measure useful independent delivery and support quality
together.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
1. CHOOSE USEFUL WORK AND CLEAR OWNERS
12
Decide what the team would do with time saved. Completing more
priority work, reducing overtime and leaving room for unexpected work
each have value, but they are different benefits. Faster execution does
not reduce cash spending while staffing and spending remain
unchanged. Chapter 3 counts saved labor time only to the extent that the
team demonstrates its use on other planned work.
Before designing the workflow, agree on the customer need, the delay to
reduce, the accountable team and the people responsible for shared
capabilities and exceptions. Those choices give the work a purpose and
make clear who can act when it fails.

13
CHAPTER 02
Build a workflow the
team can operate
Give agents current context, enforce the actions they may take, and
verify the result independently.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
2. BUILD A WORKFLOW THE TEAM CAN OPERATE
14
Maintain the context work depends on
An agent working on saved searches needs the current interface, privacy
rules, relevant product decisions and acceptance criteria. A large
collection of documents leaves the workflow maintainer with the same
question: which information should govern this task?
Context engineering is the work of managing the information available
to a model as it runs: instructions, tools, retrieved material and prior
interactions. That information needs ongoing maintenance. [S4] Every
source that can materially affect a decision needs an owner who can
correct it and decide when it is due for review.
For each task, bring together the customer goal, acceptance conditions,
relevant domain rules, current interfaces, known constraints and
reasons to escalate. Keep this packet small enough to use. Links to the
authoritative records, with the versions or retrieval times used, let a
reviewer check what the workflow relied on.
How often information needs checking depends on how quickly it
changes and the consequences of using an old version. An access policy
may need verification for every task; a stable interface example may
need review when the interface changes. The workflow maintainer
assembles the information, while the domain owner remains
responsible for its correctness.
Decide who resolves conflicting information before work starts. If an old
example permits an export that current policy forbids, stop the export
and ask the responsible owner. Correct the obsolete reference after the
decision so the next task does not encounter the same disagreement.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
2. BUILD A WORKFLOW THE TEAM CAN OPERATE
15
A failure should point to a specific correction. A missing interface
agreement needs an authoritative source; an unsupported assumption
needs clarification or a new test case. Adding every available document
can increase the amount of information the workflow has to handle
without resolving either problem.
Define a repeatable capability
To rely on a workflow, a team needs to know which tasks it can handle,
what inputs and tools it needs, how its work is checked and how to
recover from a failure. Give the complete workflow a version so
reviewers can tell what ran and reproduce the relevant conditions.
For saved searches, the capability could accept one approved interface
contract and a customer task description, propose coordinated changes
across clients and backend, and return test evidence. It should identify
unsupported work, such as a new authorization model, before execution.
A short service agreement should answer the questions a product team
will have: who maintains the workflow, who can use it, what support to
expect, how to report a defect and how to continue if it is unavailable.
Include a route for manual work and for exceptions that need a human
decision.
Choose how much freedom the task needs. A routine interface update
may follow a fixed sequence. An unfamiliar failure may require
investigation and a human decision before implementation. Use broader
agent discretion only when the surrounding controls and verification
can support the additional choices.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
2. BUILD A WORKFLOW THE TEAM CAN OPERATE
16
Fixing a product defect and changing the workflow are different
changes. The product fix belongs in the product's release record. A new
model, different tool access or a change in how agents coordinate
belongs in the workflow's version record, because it may alter what the
trial is testing.
Before a comparison begins, agree which corrections to context are
allowed and which changes require a new group of tasks to be evaluated
separately. Log every revision. If the workflow improves substantially
halfway through, combining its earlier and later results would hide the
difference.
Enforce authority through the system
Permissions need to exist in the system, not just in instructions. Decide
which actions an agent may take and enforce those limits through its
identity, tools and execution environment. Retrieved text can describe
permission, but it cannot grant access. A task asking for a production
export does not authorize one.
Containment limits what an agent can do through controls such as
sandboxes, virtual machines and network restrictions. [S6] Choose those
controls according to the consequences of the task, then check from
outside the agent that they work.
The table sets the starting permissions for this pilot. Before live work
begins, the platform owner must show that the system denies prohibited
actions, expires access and revokes it during an active run. A written
policy or an agent's refusal is not enough to establish that the system
enforces the limit.
ACTION
PERMITTED SCOPE IN THE EXAMPLE
Read
Approved repositories, documents and test data under a task
identity with limited resources and expiry.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
2. BUILD A WORKFLOW THE TEAM CAN OPERATE
17
ACTION
PERMITTED SCOPE IN THE EXAMPLE
Edit and test
An isolated branch or workspace, without production credentials.
Record changed state and test results.
Create a preview
A review environment with an owner, expiry, spending limit and
cleanup record.
Merge and release
A separately authorized person follows protected checks and the
existing release path.
Delete, export or bill
Unavailable in this pilot. A later proposal requires a separate
authority and consequence decision.
Stop and recover
The platform owner can revoke access, stop active execution, find
affected state and verify recovery.
Test the workflow and the outcome
Keep two questions separate. Can this workflow version handle
representative work? Does this delivered change solve the customer
problem? A capability evaluation addresses the first question;
independent product acceptance and customer observation address the
second.
The test set should include routine tasks, awkward but valid inputs, stale
or conflicting information, tool failures and prohibited requests. For
each case, define the expected result and inspect what actually changed
in the environment. Agent evaluation guidance distinguishes the case,
repeated trials, grading and the final outcome. [S5]
Repeat cases when variable behavior matters, and retain the result of
every case. In a synthetic suite of fifteen cases with three trials each, 41
successes out of 45 could hide one case failing all three trials. A high
aggregate can coexist with a repeatable failure.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
2. BUILD A WORKFLOW THE TEAM CAN OPERATE
18
Before the trial, decide which cases are critical and what passing each
one means. Keep the final assessment cases separate from the examples
used to tune the workflow. If an assessment case leaks into tuning, use a
replacement assessment that was defined in advance and has not been
exposed, or call the final result inconclusive. Keep the inputs, versions,
action traces, grading results and explanations of failures so someone
else can examine the result.
For each product change, test the behavior customers need and
unintended effects the task could introduce. Saved searches need
persistence and privacy checks, followed by observation of whether
customers can find and reuse the saved query. The product lead defines
representative use before delivery.
Repeating a control test tells you more about the selected scenario, not
about every situation the workflow might face. Fifteen cases run three
times still cover fifteen distinct challenges. A passing suite therefore
leaves a continuing job for production monitoring, incident response
and customer feedback.
Make the task record reviewable
A reviewer should be able to judge the work without reconstructing a
long conversation. A useful task record connects the customer goal to
the authoritative information, permitted actions and evidence needed to
accept the result.
For the saved-search example, record: "A customer can save a query,
reopen it in a later session and see a usable failure state. Saved queries
remain private to their owner." Add the test environment and
representative customer tasks that will establish those conditions.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
2. BUILD A WORKFLOW THE TEAM CAN OPERATE
19
The record needs a task ID, responsible product team, source versions,
workflow/model version, permitted resources and actions, budget,
expiry and escalation owner. Link to protected configuration rather than
copying secrets into the record. The platform owner checks that the
actual permissions match this scope.
If a backend contract contradicts a mobile example, pause the affected
work and ask the contract owner to resolve the conflict. Keep the
decision and update both references. Otherwise the team may end up
with two implementations that look compatible but follow different
requirements.
At completion, the reviewer needs links to the proposed change, actions
taken, test results and independently observed state, along with
limitations and actual effort and cost. Make clear whether the work was
proposed, executed, verified or released. Each is a different status and
needs its own evidence.
A reviewer should now be able to accept the result, request a specific
correction or escalate a decision. After release, keep the task connected
to customer observation and follow-up. If customers cannot find their
saved searches, the product team still has work to do even when the
persistence test passes.
Rehearse failure before live work
Run a stale-context conflict, an incorrect output, a tool timeout, a
prohibited request and revocation during active execution. Verify what
actually stopped, which credentials expired and what state remains. An
agent saying it stopped leaves an unanswered question if a background
job continues.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
2. BUILD A WORKFLOW THE TEAM CAN OPERATE
20
People should know who can suspend the workflow and who will restore
each affected product. Save action traces, versions and changed state
before recovery removes useful evidence. The responsible owner can
authorize a restart only after the team verifies both restoration and the
correction.
Feedback needs to reach someone who can act on it. Product defects go
to the product owner, shared workflow defects to the maintainer, and
access failures to platform/security. When a failure crosses those
responsibilities, the owners need to coordinate the response.
Budget recurring time for context corrections, evaluation updates,
provider changes and support, and include it in operating cost. Even a
useful workflow may cost too much to maintain if the work it serves
rarely occurs.
The team is ready for a comparison when it can show a real task record,
maintained context, a versioned workflow, assessment cases kept out of
tuning, enforced access and a rehearsed recovery procedure.
Unresolved gaps need owners. This preparation makes the trial possible
within its approved scope; the trial still has to show whether delivery
improves.

21
CHAPTER 03
Fund a comparison and
decide what to expand
Pay for the trial to finish, count unsuccessful work, and connect the
investment decision to confirmed customer outcomes.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
3. FUND A COMPARISON AND DECIDE WHAT TO EXPAND
22
Fund a trial that can disappoint you
All numbers and results in this chapter are synthetic. The example
follows six engineers who already use AI assistants, CI and production
controls. They are trying a workflow that combines maintained context,
tested automation and enforced permissions. The comparison tests the
combination; it cannot tell them how much benefit came from each part.
The trial covers forty-eight preference, notification and administration
changes requested to meet customer needs. It excludes authorization,
billing, destructive migrations and sensitive exports. Staffing, product
ownership and release rules stay the same. Before funding it, the
sponsor needs to know that there is enough eligible work and enough
reviewer time to finish the comparison.
The sponsor wants recurring cost per confirmed outcome at least 15%
below the current workflow, within an absolute cost ceiling, with
acceptable completion and quality. The detailed requirements in "Agree
on the investment requirements" are example investment choices. Set
locally justified requirements before enrollment.
The schedule allows weeks 1-2 to prepare and agree the trial plan, weeks
3-6 to enroll tasks, weeks 7-8 to finish delivery, and weeks 9-10 to observe
use and make the decision. Each release needs at least fourteen calendar
days of follow-up and representative customer use. Check the actual
deadlines against the business calendar before committing to this
schedule.
The sponsor approves an $86,000 cap: $16,000 for setup, $61,800 for
delivery and comparison at unchanged labor productivity, and $8,200
contingency. That contingency includes one extension to complete
missing evidence, limited to two weeks and $4,000. The budget must
cover follow-up, recovery and shutdown as well as delivery.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
3. FUND A COMPARISON AND DECIDE WHAT TO EXPAND
23
Before enrollment, the measurement owner needs statistical help to
assess how much tasks vary, the minimum gain worth pursuing and how
precisely the trial could estimate it. Document the recommended sample
size and what the trial can distinguish. Forty-eight tasks are a planning
assumption. That assessment, the funding and the recovery requirement
all need to be resolved before work enters the trial.
Keep the comparison interpretable
Compare the pilot with the team's actual current workflow, including the
AI assistants it already uses. Match twenty-four pairs of tasks by
complexity, dependencies and engineer familiarity, then randomly
assign one task in each pair to the pilot group and the other to the
comparison group. Each engineer receives four pairs. Schedule both
groups across the same weeks so a busy period or a quiet one does not
fall on only one group.
Agree task eligibility, size limits, acceptance criteria, labor rates,
severity definitions and the allocation of common costs before
enrollment, and keep them fixed. Every task stays under its original
assignment, including failures, rescues, crossover and abandonment.
Log help and reused work between groups, and give both groups the
same review priority.
The reason is practical: a pilot receiving easier tasks or priority review
could appear cheaper because the comparison was disadvantaged. Task
selection and concurrent AI work also complicate measurement in
developer research. [S7] Keep deviations visible so the readout can
explain what was tested.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
3. FUND A COMPARISON AND DECIDE WHAT TO EXPAND
24
Each change has ten business days from the time it is ready and
assigned. Waiting, blockers and rescue work all count toward that
deadline. Use the agreed business calendar and record actual
completion times, the age of unresolved tasks and late completions. Late
work still belongs in the results, even though it no longer qualifies as
timely.
An unfinished task at the deadline has no observed completion time yet.
Reporting it as completed at day ten would hide delay. Keep unfinished,
late and abandoned outcomes separate. The statistical distinction
between an observation limit and an event time is useful here; the
source note explains the analogy. [S8]
The main measure is cost per confirmed timely outcome. Waiting time,
paired results and total team output help explain that measure. With
twenty-four tasks in each group, estimates of unusually slow delivery
and differences between subgroups need caution. People in the same
team also learn from and help one another, which limits what the
comparison can establish.
Count confirmed customer outcomes
Decide what counts as success before delivery begins. In this example, a
confirmed outcome has independent production acceptance within ten
business days, remains valid through at least fourteen calendar days of
follow-up, and has the required evidence of success on representative
customer tasks. A is the count of these outcomes for each group.
A timely acceptance awaiting follow-up is pending. A late release can
still be useful, but it never enters this timely-outcome count. Remove an
accepted outcome if a predefined invalidation condition occurs, such as
a defect or customer failure making the accepted behavior unusable.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
3. FUND A COMPARISON AND DECIDE WHAT TO EXPAND
25
Every release needs observation, including late work. Before the final
decision, confirm the result for every timely acceptance and complete
quality and safety follow-up for late releases. Fourteen days without a
reported problem do not show that the change is useful; someone must
also observe the specified customer task.
One assignment register should connect each task to its original group,
pair, engineer, assignment time, deadline, production acceptance,
follow-up, customer evidence, invalidation and costs. At the end, each
task belongs in one category: confirmed timely, invalidated timely, late,
abandoned or unresolved. While the trial is running, show timely work
awaiting confirmation separately.
Account for all twenty-four assignments in each group. Fewer confirmed
outcomes mean a higher unit cost because the unsuccessful work still
cost time and money. Removing difficult tasks would make the
investment look better by hiding part of its actual burden.
When A is zero, unit cost is undefined and completion fails at final
readout. Display N/A, with the reason. Missing costs or observations
make the affected requirements Pending until resolved or the trial ends
as inconclusive. A missing result cannot be credited as a success.
Charge the complete delivery cost
For each group a, let C_a be its full recurring cost: labor at the agreed
role rates, tools, review, failures, rescues, support, maintenance, shared
measurement and outstanding recovery commitments. Keep one-time
setup S separate. Unit cost U_a = C_a / A_a; the relative cost ratio is U_P /
U_C, where P is pilot and C is comparison.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
3. FUND A COMPARISON AND DECIDE WHAT TO EXPAND
26
Charge support used by only one group to that group. Divide common
measurement costs across all assigned tasks, including unsuccessful
work. With twenty-four assignments in each group, each receives half.
Keep this allocation fixed so a lower success count cannot make
measurement costs disappear.
To see whether the trial can finish within budget, add incurred cost,
unspent commitments and work still needed but not yet committed.
Include setup, both groups, follow-up and shutdown, and reconcile
estimated usage charges with invoices. Count a commitment only once,
even if it already appears in a group's cost record.
Assume ten combined recurring labor hours per assignment, including
delivery, review, support, maintenance and common measurement. At
$125/hour, a comparison task costs 10 × $125 + $25 in tools = $1,275. The
pilot costs 10 × $125 + $50 = $1,300. The forty-eight assignments cost 24 ×
($1,275 + $1,300) = $61,800. Setup brings the no-benefit plan to $77,800.
Funding the hoped-for result would budget only $16,000 + 24 × $1,275 + 24
× $1,050 = $71,800. A $72,000 cap leaves $200 and depends on already
achieving the target. The $86,000 cap instead leaves $8,200 over the
no-benefit plan.
Review the expected cost to finish every week, including what happens
if work goes badly. Stop enrolling tasks when the remaining comparison,
follow-up and safe shutdown cannot fit within approved funding. The
trial has to remain affordable even when the hoped-for improvement
does not arrive.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
3. FUND A COMPARISON AND DECIDE WHAT TO EXPAND
27
Agree on the investment requirements
The sponsor approves the requirements and their rationale before
enrollment. The thresholds below are investment choices for this
example; they have not been statistically calibrated and do not establish
general safety. Every requirement must pass. Lower cost cannot
compensate for an unacceptable quality or control result.
Agree the severity definitions, evaluation cases and thresholds together,
and keep them fixed. If the team cannot justify a requirement or collect
the evidence for it, resolve that problem before launch. Changing a
threshold after seeing the result changes the question the trial was
meant to answer.
REQUIREMENT
EXAMPLE FINAL RULE
Recurring cost
Pilot unit cost at most $1,050 and pilot/comparison ratio at most
0.85.
Confirmed completion
At least 22/24 pilot outcomes; pilot count at least comparison count.
Engineer sensitivity
Ratio < 1 after omitting each engineer's paired work and associated
costs in turn.
Customer and quality
Complete observations; zero High/Medium incidents in either group;
pilot Low issues at most comparison Low issues + 1. Count a defect
and its rollback once.
Routine capability
15 cases × 3 trials: at least 41/45, each case at least 2/3, designated
critical cases 3/3.
Enforced controls
15 failure/control cases pass all 3 trials, including actual denial and
mid-run revocation.
Investment recovery
Complete costs, demonstrated productive reuse, modeled setup
recovery at most 12 weeks.
Comparison integrity
Every assignment retained; no preferential queue treatment,
unlogged crossover or unapproved material workflow change.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
3. FUND A COMPARISON AND DECIDE WHAT TO EXPAND
28
Read the weekly scorecard in order
The sponsor needs one consistent picture of progress. The measurement
owner prepares a cumulative snapshot at an agreed cutoff and timezone,
with delivery, product/design and platform/security owners checking
their records. Keep earlier snapshots and link corrections to them. The
sponsor records the resulting decision and actions.
For every measure, show the current and previous values, the change,
the counts used in the calculation, supporting evidence, owner and
Pass/Fail/Pending status. Calculate unit costs from cumulative totals.
Averaging weekly unit costs would give a small week the same weight as
a large one.
Start the review with controls and incidents, then ask whether the trial
can still afford to finish. Next review missing evidence, completion and
customer outcomes, quality and evaluations, and finally cost and
recovery. A promising cost ratio cannot settle a requirement while
customer follow-up is still pending.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
3. FUND A COMPARISON AND DECIDE WHAT TO EXPAND
29
 Review the scorecard in this order
1
Controls / incidents
Action and recovery traces; incident severity; routine and control results by case.
Suspend affected capability for prohibited execution, exposure or High/Medium
incidents.
2
Affordability
Incurred cost, remaining commitments and cost to finish. Preserve funds for
follow-up and shutdown.
3
Evidence / completion
All assignments, outcome states and required observations. Explain every missing
record.
4
Unit cost / sensitivity
C_a / A_a and pilot/comparison ratio; recalculate after each engineer omission.
Preserve failed-task costs.
5
Recovery / integrity
Setup, conservative net benefit, eligible demand, demonstrated capacity and
reuse; protocol deviations and version history.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
3. FUND A COMPARISON AND DECIDE WHAT TO EXPAND
30
Calculate a complete example readout
Synthetic week-ten result: all forty-eight assignments, follow-up records
and costs are resolved. Each group has twenty-three confirmed
outcomes and one abandoned change. The abandoned work remains in
cost. No outstanding commitments or further work estimates remain.
The cost and completion requirements below pass, along with quality,
evaluations and integrity. The sponsor still needs the
engineer-sensitivity and investment-recovery calculations in "Check
dependence on one engineer" and "Value capacity that was actually
reused" before deciding whether to fund another team.
MEASURE
SYNTHETIC RESULT
Recurring unit cost
Pilot $20,700 / 23 = $900. Comparison $29,900 / 23 = $1,300. Ratio
0.692; pilot cost is 30.8% lower.
Completion
23/24 in both groups, with required customer observations and
follow-up complete.
Quality
Zero High/Medium incidents. One Low pilot issue and zero
comparison Low issues; no accepted outcome invalidated.
Evaluations
Routine 44/45; every case at least 2/3, critical cases 3/3. Controls
45/45 across all 15 cases.
Total funding used
$16,000 setup + $20,700 pilot + $29,900 comparison = $66,600.
Remaining headroom: $19,400.
Integrity
No prohibited execution, preferential review, unlogged crossover or
unapproved material workflow change.
Check dependence on one engineer
An aggregate improvement may depend heavily on one person's work.
Recalculate the result after removing each engineer's paired
assignments and associated costs from both groups. This sensitivity
check asks whether the direction survives that omission.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
3. FUND A COMPARISON AND DECIDE WHAT TO EXPAND
31
In the synthetic readout, the six engineers contribute [4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 3]
confirmed outcomes in each group. Pilot costs are [$3,600, $3,600, $3,600,
$3,600, $3,600, $2,700]. Comparison costs are [$5,200, $5,200, $5,200,
$5,200, $5,200, $3,900]. All include unsuccessful work and allocated
support.
Omitting any engineer with four outcomes leaves nineteen per group,
$17,100 pilot cost and $24,700 comparison cost. Unit costs remain $900
and $1,300. Omitting the engineer with three outcomes leaves twenty per
group, $18,000 and $26,000. The same unit costs remain.
All six omission ratios are 0.692, below the example requirement of 1.
The cost advantage remains when any one engineer's work is left out.
Keep the task and cost records linked to each engineer so another
reviewer can reproduce the calculation.
The check does not produce a confidence interval, isolate the workflow's
components or remove shared learning between engineers. Similar
tasks, common review and within-team assistance still constrain
interpretation. A second team is a new test of operation, support and
economics.
If omitting one engineer reverses the result, investigate that dependence
before expansion. The result may point to expertise the workflow has
not yet made reusable. Treat that explanation as a hypothesis for the
next design, while retaining the original failed requirement.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
3. FUND A COMPARISON AND DECIDE WHAT TO EXPAND
32
Value capacity that was actually reused
In this example, saved time counts toward paying back setup only when
the team uses it for other planned work. That value and any nonlabor
savings must cover setup to meet the investment rule. Let L be
comparison minus pilot labor cost per confirmed outcome, and N the
corresponding nonlabor difference. When L is positive, q is the share of
that saving backed by completed work, capped between zero and one.
Count priority work that was named in advance and completed without
extra staffing or overtime, supported by effort records for the people
involved. Check those records against the main cost records to avoid
counting the same work twice. This estimates the value of capacity used;
it does not show that cash spending fell.
The conservative net benefit is B = min(L, 0) + q × max(L, 0) + N. Any
increase in labor cost counts in full; a labor saving counts only in
proportion to demonstrated reuse. Let V be the lower of eligible weekly
demand over the trailing eight weeks and confirmed pilot outcomes
divided by six delivery weeks. Modeled recovery time is S / (B × V).
In the synthetic case, comparison labor is 230 hours and pilot labor is
150, all at $125/hour. Estimated released time is 23 × (230/23) - 150 = 80
hours. All eighty have demonstrated productive reuse, so q = 1. Labor
costs are $28,750 and $18,750; nonlabor costs are $1,150 and $1,950.
B = ($10,000 - $800) / 23 = $400. Demand is six per week, but demonstrated
pilot capacity is 23/6 = 3.83. Recovery is $16,000 / ($400 × 23/6) = 10.4
weeks, within the twelve-week rule. Keep capacity at the demonstrated
rate rather than doubling it for assumed full-team adoption.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
3. FUND A COMPARISON AND DECIDE WHAT TO EXPAND
33
This forecast begins after adoption and counts no benefit from the pilot
period. It estimates payback; the team has not observed it yet. If only
sixty of eighty hours have demonstrated reuse, q = 0.75: B = ($7,500 -
$800)/23 = $291.30 and recovery takes 14.3 weeks. If B or V is nonpositive,
no finite recovery exists.
Distinguish missing evidence
from failure
At the planned week-ten review, a complete result that passes every
requirement can support one separately funded trial with a second team.
A complete result that fails a requirement stops expansion. A sponsor
may believe a revised workflow would do better, but that is a reason for
a new proposal, not for changing this result.
If a customer observation is missing, mark the affected outcome and
calculations Pending. The single extension to complete evidence is
available only if no completed requirement has failed, every
requirement unaffected by that observation passes, the observation is
scheduled and finishing fits within the cap. Calculations that depend on
the observation remain Pending. Keep the workflow and thresholds
fixed, along with the original readout, so the extension completes the
same comparison.
A completed cost failure needs a different decision. Suppose pilot cost is
$25,300 for twenty-three confirmed outcomes: $1,100 each. Relative cost
is $1,100/$1,300 = 0.846, which passes the relative threshold but fails the
$1,050 ceiling. Even with full reuse, $200 benefit per outcome gives
recovery of 20.9 weeks. Stop expansion.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
3. FUND A COMPARISON AND DECIDE WHAT TO EXPAND
34
If required evidence is still missing at week twelve, close the trial as
inconclusive. Explain what could not be observed and keep its costs in
the result. A fresh intervention needs a new charter. Extending the same
trial repeatedly until a favorable result appears would undermine the
decision the sponsor agreed to make.
A prohibited action, data exposure or High/Medium incident requires
immediate suspension of the affected capability. Revoke access, contain
the incident, preserve evidence and verify recovery. An uncorrectable
control failure or unaffordable completion ends the pilot.
Calibrate economics before launch. At the planning ceiling of $1,050
against $1,275, the difference is $225. Even with full reuse and four
outcomes weekly, $16,000 setup takes 17.8 weeks to recover. A cost target
alone cannot guarantee the separate recovery requirement.
Expand one commitment at a time
In the synthetic example, every requirement passed. The sponsor can
consider funding one second team with the same task scope and
permissions, named owners and a recorded reason for the decision.
The second team needs to establish its own onboarding cost, specialist
access, support needs, customer outcomes and sustainable delivery
capacity, including maintenance and absences. It may not be able to get
the champions' help at the original team's cost.
Consider four expansion decisions separately: more work for the same
team, another team, broader permissions and changed staffing. More
volume tests review and support capacity; another team tests whether
the workflow travels well; broader access changes the consequences of
failure; and staffing changes affect expertise and recovery.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
3. FUND A COMPARISON AND DECIDE WHAT TO EXPAND
35
Say what is changing and what evidence would justify it before
committing. A successful low-risk implementation trial does not
authorize sensitive exports. A recurring capacity benefit alone cannot
justify reducing specialist coverage.
Keep the prior workflow and a recovery route while learning. Stop or
narrow the investment if cost, customer outcomes or support burden no
longer meet the approved criteria. Disappointing findings belong in the
next decision too.
Use the worksheets to agree on the customer need, intervention, owners,
permissions, full budget and decision requirements before enrollment.
The purpose is to make a better investment decision. Expand when the
evidence supports the next commitment and the customer outcome
remains worth pursuing.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
3. FUND A COMPARISON AND DECIDE WHAT TO EXPAND
36
Working tools
A. Write the launch record
Complete this record in the team's source of truth before enrollment. Use
names, dates, actual values and links to enforceable configuration.
Resolve gaps before the sponsor funds live work.
DECISION TO RECORD
LOCAL ANSWER REQUIRED
Useful work
Customer need; observed dependency; eligible task class and
exclusions; current workflow; proposed intervention.
Responsibility
Named product, design, specialist, workflow, platform/security,
measurement and sponsor owners; reserved time and absence
coverage.
Task evidence
Acceptance and invalidation rules; representative customer tasks;
deadlines, calendar and follow-up; independent verification.
Authority
Resources, permitted actions, expiry and spending; actual
denial/revocation tests; incident and recovery owners.
Comparison
Pairing and assignment; queue treatment; assistance/crossover
records; frozen versions and permitted corrections; sample
adequacy rationale.
Full funding
Setup, no-benefit delivery cost, maintenance, measurement, adverse
cases, contingency and safe shutdown; cost allocation and rates.
Final decision
Justified thresholds, evidence owners, readout date, one permitted
extension, suspension/stop rules and exact replication scope.
B. Record the weekly decision
1. Freeze the cutoff, timezone, workflow version and assignment
register. Keep earlier snapshots and link corrections to the record they
change.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
WORKING TOOLS
37
2. Reconcile incidents, action traces and control tests first. Record
suspension and recovery decisions with their owners. Check that access
and execution actually stopped when required.
3. Update incurred cost, accruals, unspent commitments and cost to
finish. Keep setup separate and count commitments once. Reserve funds
through final follow-up and safe shutdown.
4. Reconcile every assignment to its outcome state. Link independent
acceptance, representative customer observation and follow-up. Explain
missing evidence and name its owner and resolution date.
5. Calculate cumulative unit costs, comparison ratio, confirmed
completion, engineer sensitivity and modeled recovery. Show
current/prior values, deltas and Pass/Fail/Pending. Explain every
undefined value.
6. Review evaluation cases, review waiting, help between groups,
version changes and protocol exceptions. Preserve failures and
unsuccessful-task costs in the same snapshot as the apparent gains.
7. Record the calculated recommendation, sponsor decision, reasons and
actions with owners and dates. At final readout, preserve a complete
inventory of work, costs, observations, failures and decisions. State the
conclusions the comparison can support and the new evidence required
for expansion.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
WORKING TOOLS
38
Notes and sources
Evidence behind the recommendations
The recommendations in this handbook bring together ideas about team
responsibility, shared expertise and controlled experiments. The task
agreements, ownership rules, worksheets and expansion sequence are
my synthesis. They have not been tested together as an organizational
model.
Two historical accounts inform the approach. Spotify's 2012 account
describes squads with delivery responsibility, specialist chapters and
wider guilds [S1]. Stine connects autonomous delivery with self-service
infrastructure, automation and recovery [S2]. Both describe their
original settings; neither establishes an AI productivity result.
Saha proposes product builders supported by reusable specialist agent
capabilities and a shared platform [S3], and explicitly calls for
experimentation. His proposal informs the ownership and operating
decisions in Chapters 1-2. It is a starting point to test, rather than
evidence that this way of organizing has succeeded.
Provider guidance informs the discussion of execution context [S4],
evaluation structure [S5] and containment [S6]. The arrangements for
source ownership, service agreements and numerical requirements are
recommendations made here. The technical guidance does not establish
their effect on an organization.

AI-NATIVE ORGANIZATION HANDBOOK
NOTES AND SOURCES
39

concurrent AI measurement [S7]. NIST distinguishes the limit of an
observation from an observed event time in reliability data [S8]; "Keep
the comparison interpretable" borrows that distinction to explain
unfinished work. DORA supports small batches and short feedback
cycles [S9]. These sources inform the trial design, but none provides an
estimate of its benefit.
The four company-scale arrangements in "Match the structure to your
coordination needs" are also proposals. Team Topologies distinguishes
outcome-aligned teams, enabling support, specialist work and platforms
[S10]. CNCF describes platforms shaped around internal users [S11].
Google Cloud supplies a cloud-specific example of shared foundations
with separate business-unit and application responsibilities [S12]. These
sources inform the distinctions; none establishes the four headcounts as
transition rules.
Every Chapter 3 plan and result is synthetic. Research cutoff: October 23,
